item.title: [SCS 2025] When Aztec Scholars Wrote in Latin: The Award-Winning Book That Redraws the Map of the Renaissance
item.body:
> Andrew Laird's book "Aztec Latin," honored with the Society for Classical Studies' 2025 Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit, shows how Indigenous Nahua scholars in 16th-century Mexico mastered Latin and helped create a remarkable hybrid literature — one that historians long overlooked.

## What Was Presented

At its 2025 Annual Meeting, the Society for Classical Studies (SCS) — the leading North American association for the study of ancient Greece and Rome — awarded its Charles J. Goodwin Award of Merit to Andrew Laird, a classicist at Brown University, for his book *Aztec Latin: Renaissance Learning and Nahuatl Traditions in Early Colonial Mexico* (Oxford University Press). The Goodwin Award recognizes outstanding contributions to classical scholarship, and the award committee called the book "in many ways a truly pioneering work."

The story it tells begins in 1536, only fifteen years after the fall of the Aztec Empire. Franciscan missionaries founded the Colegio de Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco (central Mexico) — the first European-style institution of higher learning in the Americas — and began teaching Latin, classical rhetoric, and Aristotelian philosophy to Indigenous youths.

What happened next was not a one-way transfer of European culture. Laird documents an extraordinary two-way exchange. Friars applied the rules of Latin grammar to describe and record Amerindian languages such as Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. Meanwhile, Nahua students became accomplished Latinists in their own right: they translated the Gospels, devotional literature, and even Aesop's fables into Nahuatl, wrote petitions in polished Latin addressed to European rulers, and collaborated on landmark projects such as the Florentine Codex, the encyclopedic record of Aztec culture compiled with the friar Bernardino de Sahagún.

Across nine chapters of case studies — covering rhetoric, grammar, translation, Latin letters, and native chronicles — Laird argues that these Indigenous scholars were genuine intellectual agents whose contributions were substantial but historically overshadowed. The result of their work, he shows, was not imitation of Europe but a new literature of unusual complexity, born from the meeting of Renaissance humanism and Nahuatl traditions.

## Why It Matters

For most readers, "the Renaissance" conjures Florence, Rome, and European libraries. This book widens that picture dramatically: within a generation of the conquest, some of the most sophisticated Latin scholarship in the world was being produced in the Americas, much of it by Indigenous writers. That changes how we think about who "owns" the classical tradition.

It also matters for how scholars study the ancient world today. Classics has been asking hard questions about its colonial entanglements, and Laird's work is a model of how to face them: he examines both the violence of colonialism and the creativity of the people who lived through it, and he cautions against assuming that the Greek and Roman classics must always sit at the center of the story. Reviewers — from the Bryn Mawr Classical Review to the Times Literary Supplement — have highlighted exactly this balance.

Finally, the book restores names and voices. The Nahua Latinists of Tlatelolco were long treated as footnotes to the missionaries who taught them. Recovering their role is a reminder that cultural encounters, even under brutally unequal conditions, are rarely as one-sided as the winners' histories suggest.

## An Easy Way to Understand It

Think of it like a musical collaboration. Imagine European teachers arriving with sheet music and classical instruments, expecting local musicians simply to play the old European repertoire. Instead, the Nahua students learned the new instruments fluently — and then used them to perform their own melodies, and to write entirely new songs that neither side could have composed alone. "Aztec Latin" is the story of that unexpected album: European in its notation, Mexican in much of its voice, and genuinely new as a whole.

## Three-Line Summary

1. Andrew Laird's *Aztec Latin* won the SCS 2025 Goodwin Award of Merit for showing how Renaissance learning and Nahuatl culture met in 16th-century Mexico.
2. From 1536, Indigenous students at the Colegio de Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco mastered Latin and rhetoric, translating Gospels and Aesop's fables into Nahuatl and writing Latin petitions to European rulers.
3. The book argues this was a two-way exchange that produced a complex hybrid literature — and that its Indigenous authors deserve a central place in the history of the classical tradition.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Society for Classical Studies (SCS)**: The principal North American scholarly association for the study of ancient Greek and Roman civilization; its Goodwin Award honors outstanding books in the field.
- **Nahuatl**: The language of the Aztecs and many other peoples of central Mexico, still spoken today by over a million people.
- **Renaissance humanism**: A European educational movement centered on classical languages, eloquence, and the study of ancient texts, which missionaries carried to the Americas.
- **Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco**: A school founded by Franciscans in 1536 near Mexico City — the first European-style institution of higher learning in the Americas, where Nahua students studied Latin, rhetoric, and philosophy.
- **Florentine Codex**: A monumental 16th-century encyclopedia of Aztec history and culture, compiled by friar Bernardino de Sahagún together with Indigenous scholars, written in Nahuatl and Spanish.
